When we cannot solve the score equation $\score(\th) = 0$ algebraically,
we can search for its solution numerically [@dobson4e, Chapter 4].
The **Newton-Raphson algorithm** starts from an initial guess $\esttmp{\th}$
and repeats the update

$$
\begin{aligned}
\esttmp{\th}
&\leftarrow \esttmp{\th} - \inv{\hessf{\vx; \esttmp{\th}}} \scoref{\vx; \esttmp{\th}}\\
&= \esttmp{\th} + \inv{\oinff{\vx; \esttmp{\th}}} \scoref{\vx; \esttmp{\th}}
\end{aligned}
$$

until the estimate stops changing,
where the second line uses $\oinf = -\hess$
([observed information](#def-oinf)).

{{< slidebreak >}}

The update comes from approximating the score function near $\esttmp{\th}$
by its first-order
[Taylor polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor%27s_theorem):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\score(\th)
&\approx \score^*(\th)\\
&\eqdef \score(\esttmp{\th}) + \hess(\esttmp{\th})(\th - \esttmp{\th})
\end{aligned}
$$

The approximate score function $\score^*(\th)$ is linear in $\th$,
so the approximate score equation $\score^*(\th) = 0$
is easy to solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \score(\esttmp{\th}) + \hess(\esttmp{\th})(\th - \esttmp{\th})
&& \text{(set $\score^*(\th) = 0$)}\\
-\score(\esttmp{\th}) &= \hess(\esttmp{\th})(\th - \esttmp{\th})
&& \text{(subtract $\score(\esttmp{\th})$)}\\
-\inv{\hess(\esttmp{\th})}\score(\esttmp{\th}) &= \th - \esttmp{\th}
&& \text{(multiply by $\inv{\hess(\esttmp{\th})}$ on the left)}\\
\th &= \esttmp{\th} - \inv{\hess(\esttmp{\th})}\score(\esttmp{\th})
&& \text{(add $\esttmp{\th}$)}
\end{aligned}
$$

and the solution becomes the next guess.

{{< slidebreak >}}

**Fisher scoring** (also called the method of scoring)
replaces the observed information $\oinf(\vx; \esttmp{\th})$ in the update
with the [expected information](#def-einf) $\einf(\esttmp{\th})$,
which is sometimes simpler to compute:

$$
\esttmp{\th} \leftarrow \esttmp{\th} + \inv{\einff{\esttmp{\th}}} \scoref{\vx; \esttmp{\th}}
$$


{{< slidebreak >}}

A third option is the **empirical information matrix**
[@mclachlan2007em]:

$$
\oinf_e(\th; \vx) \eqdef
\sum_{i = 1}^{n} \score_i \tp{\score_i}
- \frac{1}{n} \score \tp{\score}
$$

where $\score_i$ is the score of the $i$th observation's log-likelihood,
and $\score = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \score_i$.
For $\iid$ data, $\frac{1}{n}\oinf_e(\th; \vx)$
is the sample covariance matrix (with divisor $n$)
of the observations' scores,
so it estimates the covariance matrix of one observation's score,
$\einf(\th)/n$
(@thm-information-equality).
The empirical information needs only first derivatives,
so it can be easier to compute than the observed information.
